context_line: Informal hello to one person you call tu: a friend, a child, family. Not for an elder, a boss or a stranger; to them say Laba diena. It is also the first word of labas rytas / laba diena / labas vakaras.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §2.1, §2.5: 'Vyresniam už save asmeniui, viršininkui, profesoriui nederėtų sakyti net vieną sveikinimosi žodį labas ar sveikas'; also lt.wiktionary 'labas': 'sakoma sveikinantis (neformaliai)'

context_line: Plural of sveikas: hello to several people, or to one person you call jūs. Neutral and common in shops and offices, but still a one-word greeting: with an elder or a superior Laba diena is the safer choice.
source_note: en.wiktionary 'sveiki' (to more than one person) and 'sveikas' (informal, to a male); Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §2.1 (Sveikas, drauguži! Sveiki, vaikai!) and §2.5 (labas/sveikas not to superiors). The jūs-singular use of Sveiki is everyday practice but not stated in a source I could read — hence medium.

context_line: Good morning, on first meeting in the morning; to anyone, tu or jūs. At home the one who gets up later greets those already up. Labą rytą (accusative) is equally correct.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §2.1 (both cases correct, nominative preferred), §2.5 (family custom)

context_line: Good day: the all-purpose polite daytime greeting for shops, offices, strangers and anyone you call jūs. Use it where labas would be too familiar. Labą dieną is equally correct.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §2.1, §2.5. VLKK consultation 8094 'laba diena / gera diena' exists (https://www.vlkk.lt/konsultacijos/8094-laba-diena-gera-diena-labintis-pasilabinti) but vlkk.lt could not be fetched from this session (Cloudflare challenge); title only.

context_line: Good evening, said on meeting in the evening (arriving at a door, entering a shop late in the day). When parting for the night the word is labanakt, not labas vakaras.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §2.1 lists labas vakaras among greetings; §3 places labanakt(is) at parting 'vakare, prieš naktį'

context_line: Good night: only when parting for the night or going to bed, never on arrival. Short for labanaktis; fits everyone and every occasion. The diminutive labos naktelės is familiar.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §3: 'labanaktis ar trumpesnė jo forma labanakt tinka visiems ir visais atvejais'; also en.wiktionary 'labanaktis'

context_line: Goodbye: the neutral everyday farewell, accepted standard, fits anyone. Viso labo is the more Lithuanian variant; the clipped viso! is teenage talk; viso geriausio is familiar and not for people you respect.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §3

context_line: Goodbye, the old word (from su Dievu, 'with God'). The etiquette guide calls it the best and most Lithuanian farewell; it faded under Soviet anti-religious pressure, and many speakers now keep it for long or final partings.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §3 ('Geriausia, lietuviškiausia atsisveikinti… sudiev! arba sudie!'); Jasiūnaitė 1997 §29 on its decline under atheist propaganda (https://journals.vu.lt/kalbotyra/article/download/31319/30283/73015); 'final partings' rests on en.wiktionary 'sudie' glossing 'adieu' — medium.

context_line: See you (till we meet). Accepted standard, but the etiquette guide classes it with iki vakaro / iki rytojaus as a farewell for people you are close to; broadcasters also use it to an audience.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §3: 'Tokius atsisveikinimus galime tarti tik artimiems žmonėms… Atsisveikinam iki kito karto!'

context_line: Bye: the one-word farewell between friends, favoured by teenagers and young people. Fine in its place; not for a stranger, an elder or a superior.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §3: 'Su draugais kartais lakoniškai atsisveikiname tik vienu žodžiu iki… paauglių, jaunuolių mėgstami'; en.wiktionary 'iki' (interjection: bye)

context_line: See you tomorrow: iki + genitive, like iki vakaro, iki susitikimo. Same register as iki pasimatymo — people you know; to a stranger say viso gero.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §3

context_line: Thank you. Ačiū and dėkui are exact synonyms in every register. The replies: prašom (warm) or nėra už ką (modest). An answer to 'how are you?' begins with it: Ačiū, gerai.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §6.2 ('absoliučiais sinonimais'), §6.3 (replies), §6.2 end (Ačiū, gerai!)

context_line: Thanks — but not more casual than ačiū: the two are exact synonyms, both standard and both spoken. Dėkui is the one with a family: dėkoti, padėka, dėkingas.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §6.2. Note for the owner: the deck's gloss 'thanks' hints at a register difference the reference denies.

context_line: Thank you very much: labai ačiū / labai dėkui is the correct intensifier (didelis ačiū is a Russian calque to avoid); labai labai ačiū for real gratitude. Dėkoju or esu labai dėkingas are politer still.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §6.2

context_line: Please / you're welcome: 1st person singular of prašyti. The cooler, more official of the pair — at home in requests and orders (Prašau pranešti…). As a reply to thanks or when handing something over, prašom is warmer and more usual. Put it before the verb, never after (not 'Pasakykit, prašau').
source_note: en.wiktionary 'prašom' usage notes (citing VLKK 9416 'prašom, prašau, prašyčiau…', https://www.vlkk.lt/konsultacijos/9416-prasom-prasau-prasyciau-prasome-prasytume — not fetched, Cloudflare); Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §7.1–7.3

context_line: Here you are / please / you're welcome: the warm, hospitable form — inviting someone in, offering food, handing something over, and the usual reply to ačiū. Grammatically plural but said by one speaker; more common than prašau in speech.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §6.3, §7.1; en.wiktionary 'prašom' (Balčikonis recommended prašom over prašau)

context_line: You're welcome / not at all (lit. 'there is nothing for'): the modest folk reply to thanks, playing the favour down. Prašom is the other reply, fitting when the favour was real. Informal: nėr už ką.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §6.3 ('Yra dar liaudiškas atsakymas dėkojančiam: Nėr už ką!'); en.wiktionary 'nėra už ką'

context_line: No problem / it's nothing: the reply to someone's atsiprašau after a bump or a small mishap — said quietly with a nod (Nieko! or Nieko tokio!). Never answer an apology with prašau. Not a reply to thanks.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §7.4: 'Palenkiant galvą, tinka… atsakyti: Nieko! (Nieko tokio!)'; prašau in that slot 'išeina nei šis, nei tas'

context_line: It's nothing / never mind (lit. 'nothing terrible'): fills the same slot as nieko tokio, reassuring someone who apologises or worries.
source_note: No source read states this phrase; en.wiktionary has no entry (404). The etiquette guide gives only Nieko! / Nieko tokio! in the apology-reply slot.

context_line: Excuse me (to get attention or to get past): 1st person 'I apologise', so it fits tu and jūs alike. The standard opener to a stranger: Atsiprašau! Gal galėtumėt pasakyti…. When it means 'let me through', the reply is prašom.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §7.4, §8.1–8.2; en.wiktionary 'atsiprašau' ('request for attention, to pass or for an apology')

context_line: I'm sorry: the same word as the excuse-me, now an apology after the fact (a bump, a broken cup). The other person answers Nieko (tokio), not prašau. To say what for: Atsiprašau už….
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §7.4; lt.wiktionary 'atsiprašyti' example 'Atsiprašau už įžeidimą'

context_line: Excuse me / forgive me, formal: imperative of atleisti 'to forgive' in the jūs form (to a tu-person: Atleisk). It asks pardon rather than announcing an apology, so it sounds a shade weightier than atsiprašau; also when you have forgotten something: Atleiskit, išdilo iš atminties.
source_note: en.wiktionary 'atleisti' (to forgive, pardon); Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §10.1 example; Wikivoyage phrasebook (https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Lithuanian_phrasebook) gives Atleiskite for 'excuse me (begging pardon)' and 'I'm sorry'

context_line: Can you help me? Indicative galite (jūs): direct, fine with service staff. The conditional galėtumėte (next card) is the gentler form the etiquette guide recommends to strangers and elders, usually with gal: Gal galėtumėt….
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §8.1

context_line: Could you help me? Conditional mood, the politest request. 'Gal galėtumėt…' is singled out as very polite and very gentle — for a stranger, an elder or anyone you respect.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §8.1: 'dalelytė gal kartu su tariamosios nuosakos veiksmažodžiu galėtumėt labai mandagiai, labai švelniai išreiškia kreipimąsi į nepažįstamą vyresnį ar šiaip gerbtiną žmogų'

context_line: How old are you?, the jūs form: respect, formality, distance. To a child or a friend: Kiek tau metų? (sentence card S-0051). Young Lithuanians themselves often hesitate between tu and jūs.
source_note: Ivanauskaitė & Hilbig 2023, Taikomoji kalbotyra 19: plural address = respect, formality, polite distance; singular = friendliness, intimacy, familiarity

context_line: How old are you?, the tu form: for a child, a friend, family. Tu signals friendliness and closeness; to an adult you don't know, use jūs: Kiek jums metų?
source_note: Ivanauskaitė & Hilbig 2023 (as above). Sentence note type — field to be decided by the executor.

context_line: How are you? (how is it going), asked of people you know. The answer begins with thanks: Ačiū, gerai.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §6.2 end: 'Atsakymą visuomet turime pradėti padėkos žodžiu: Ačiū (dėkui), gerai!' The tu/jūs register of Kaip sekasi itself is not stated in a source read.

context_line: I'm fine. In full, Ačiū, gerai: Lithuanian etiquette starts the answer to 'how are you?' with a word of thanks.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §6.2 end

context_line: Nice to meet you (lit. 'pleasant to get acquainted'), said on being introduced. The younger or less senior person introduces themselves first, a man before a woman; in a formal meeting give your surname, not only your first name.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §10.1; en.wiktionary 'malonu' (Malonu susipažinti su jumis)

context_line: Welcome! (lit. 'healthy, having arrived'): the set phrase for guests who have travelled to you. Plural form, used to one person or many. For someone already at the door, Prašom! or Užeikite! invites them in.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §2.1: 'Iš toliau atkeliavę svečiai sveikinami žodžių junginiu sveiki atvykę!'; §7.3 on prašom at the door

context_line: Come in! — jūs imperative (Užeik! to a tu-person). The etiquette guide prefers a plain Prašom! at the door and marks 'Įeikit(e), prašau!' as rude.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §7.3 discusses įeikite, not užeikite; the transfer to užeikite is mine.

context_line: Hello, on the telephone only, when answering a private line (Klausau, 'I'm listening', is the other). At a workplace answer with the office or your name, not alio.
source_note: Kniūkšta (ed.), Kompiuterinis lietuvių kalbos žinynas, ch. 'Kalbos etiketas' (Šviesa 2004) §11: 'Ar visada tinka telefonu atsakyti žodžiu klausau arba alio? Ne, ne visada!'
